title: Concupiscence is sin broadly (ψεικτόν); strict forensic sense distinguished (Davenant/Augustine)
source_text: XXIII. Nam istam concupiscentiam peccatum merito appellari contendunt, quoniam est aliquid malum in genere morum, Deo displicens atque odiosum, quodque rationi & legi divinae adversatur, & ab ordine a Deo in ipsa creatione constituto recedit. Quippe peccatum in genere, istis est qualibet mala dispositio, vel actio creaturae rationalis sua natura repugnans alicui legi creatoris, quae aut indita, aut praescripta fuit eidem creaturae. Ideoque pravas dispositiones, & vitiosos habitus, seu innatos, sive acquisitos, in fidelibus ipsis post justificationem eorum residuos, peccati rationem & naturam habere docent, quatenus personam in qua reperiuntur afficiunt modo contrario illi qui fuit a Deo in prima creatione positus: & sunt aliquid ψεκτόν, id est, vituperabile & malum, non simpliciter Physicum, sed Morale; quod cum peccato, in tota sua latitudine sumpto, converti & reciprocum esse censent. Concedunt tamen concupiscentiam quae in ipsis regenitis haeret non esse peccatum strictissima hujus vocis significatione, juxta quam peccatum quandoque, & ab Augustino praesertim, significat Malum ex ordinatione divina puniendum, & quod personam in qua reperitur in judicio divino ream actu constituit, & ad poenam obligat: ut videre est apud Joannem Davenantium, de Justitia habituali, cap. 9. & 13. Ubi distinguit, ut jam expositum est, peccatum in latius & strictius sic dictum; atque utitur ista distinctione ut conciliet dicta quaedam Augustini, quae in speciem contraria videntur, nempe, in quibus modo negat, modo affirmat concupiscentiam, quae in renatis manet, esse peccatum.
pass_a_gloss: For they contend that that concupiscence is deservedly called sin, because it is something evil in the moral genus, displeasing and hateful to God, which is contrary to reason and the divine law, and recedes from the order constituted by God in creation itself. For sin in general, for them, is any evil disposition or action of a rational creature by its nature repugnant to some law of the creator which was either implanted in or prescribed to that creature. And therefore they teach that evil dispositions and vicious habits, whether innate or acquired, remaining in the faithful themselves after their justification, have the character and nature of sin, inasmuch as they affect the person in whom they are found in a manner contrary to that which was set by God in the first creation: and they are something ψεκτόν, that is, blameworthy and evil, not simply Physical but Moral; which they judge convertible and reciprocal with sin taken in its whole breadth. Yet they concede that the concupiscence which clings in the regenerate themselves is not sin in the strictest signification of this word, according to which sin sometimes, and especially by Augustine, signifies an Evil to be punished by divine ordination, and which actually constitutes the person in whom it is found guilty in the divine judgment and obliges to penalty: as may be seen in John Davenant, On Habitual Righteousness, chapters 9 and 13. Where he distinguishes, as already explained, sin more broadly and more strictly so called; and uses that distinction to reconcile certain sayings of Augustine that seem contrary in appearance, namely those in which he sometimes denies, sometimes affirms, that the concupiscence which remains in the regenerate is sin.
pass_b_english: Reformed call remaining concupiscence sin in the broad moral sense—blameworthy ψεκτόν against creation's order.
Strictly (Augustine/Davenant) it is not always forensic guilt-obliging sin; the broad/strict distinction reconciles Augustine.
